GNS3: Home GNS3 / Routed Lab Network emulation · QEMU nodes, routes, proof GNS3: building a routed lab that actually routes GNS3 draws the topology; you build the routing. This page is the part the diagrams skip: how to create QEMU nodes that boot reliably, how to address every link so two nodes agree on a subnet, how to add static and OSPF routes, how to get out to the internet without leaking lab traffic, and how to prove the path with counters instead of hope. KVM accelerated static + OSPF link capture 4-node topology 01 Emulation, not simulation Packet Tracer simulates; GNS3 runs real operating systems and real routing daemons. That means real kernel behaviour, real bugs, and real resource cost. Choose the node type by what you are testing. Node type What runs Use it for Cost QEMU VM A full OS image on KVM Linux routers, firewalls, appliances, anything with a kernel RAM and CPU per node Docker A container on the GNS3 host Quick Linux endpoints and services Shares the host kernel Ethernet switch Virtual switch with ports Layer-2 labs, VLAN tagging Nearly free Cloud / NAT node A bridge to the host Reaching the LAN or the internet Easy to misconfigure The rules of a routed lab are boring and absolute: every link is its own subnet, every node knows the subnet of its own interfaces, and every node has a route for everything it cannot reach directly. When that is true, ping works; when it is not, no amount of GNS3 icons will help. 02 Install the server and the GUI Two shapes: the GNS3 VM (a packaged server, required for QEMU on Windows and macOS) or a headless gns3-server on Linux, with the GUI talking to it over HTTP. The headless shape is easier to back up and to keep off the internet. sudo apt update sudo apt install -y gns3-server gns3-gui qemu-system-x86 qemu-utils \\ libvirt-daemon-system ovs-vswitchd gns3server --version systemctl --user status gns3-server 2>/dev/null | head -5 ss -ltnp | grep 3080 # the API port; keep it on 127.0.0.1 # KVM present, and usable by your user kvm-ok 2>/dev/null || egrep -c "(vmx|svm)" /proc/cpuinfo ls -l /dev/kvm No KVM, no lab Without /dev/kvm access, QEMU falls back to software emulation and a four-node lab crawls. Add your user to the kvm group, or run the GNS3 server as the user who owns the images — and never on a host where you also run production VMs you care about. Bind the server to 127.0.0.1 in the server config unless you are deliberately running it headless on another machine, and keep that machine on a management network, not on the internet. 03 Design before you click Write the addressing plan first. It is the only part of the lab that cannot be fixed by clicking harder, and it is what makes a route table readable. Segment Subnet Nodes Purpose transit-a 10.10.1.0/30 r1 .1, r2 .2 Point-to-point link, only two usable addresses transit-b 10.10.2.0/30 r2 .1, r3 .2 Second hop of the path lan-1 10.10.11.0/24 r1 .1, host .10 Where the client lives lan-3 10.10.13.0/24 r3 .1, host .10 Destination segment mgmt GNS3 internal Server only The GUI and console traffic, never routed into the lab Four nodes are enough to learn everything on this page: r1 and r2 and r3 as routers, plus one host. Draw it on paper, then reproduce it. The diagram is documentation, not decoration. 04 QEMU nodes: disk, console, adapters Create the image once, boot it outside GNS3 to install the OS, then register it as a template. Booting inside GNS3 first is how people lose an afternoon to a black console. # one disk per node role, thin-provisioned qemu-img create -f qcow2 r1.qcow2 8G # install the OS outside GNS3: serial console, one virtio NIC qemu-system-x86_64 -enable-kvm -m 512 -smp 2 \ -drive file=r1.qcow2,if=virtio \ -netdev user,id=n0 -device virtio-net-pci,netdev=n0 \ -nographic Template field Value Why Binary qemu-system-x86_64 Match the architecture of the image RAM / CPUs 512 MB, 2 vCPU for a router Four routers must fit in the host's budget Adapters virtio-net-pci , count set explicitly The count must equal the links you will draw Console Telnet with -nographic , or VNC Telnet needs a serial console configured in the guest Options -enable-kvm -smp 2 Without KVM the lab is unusable Disk Per-node qcow2 copy Nodes must not share a writable disk Serial console, or you cannot log in Add console=ttyS0 to the kernel command line (and enable a getty on it) before you register the template. GNS3's telnet console is a serial line: without a getty, you get a blank screen and assume the node failed. 05 Addressing and the first route GNS3 connects cables; it does not assign addresses. Configure each interface inside the guest, with the subnet from your plan, then verify before adding more. # inside r1 sudo ip addr add 10.10.1.1/30 dev ens3 sudo ip addr add 10.10.11.1/24 dev ens4 sudo ip link set ens3 up && sudo ip link set ens4 up sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 # make it survive a reboot echo 'net.ipv4.ip_forward=1' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-lab.conf ip -br addr ip route ping -c2 10.10.11.10 # the host on the LAN segment Two details catch almost everyone: the /30 on a point-to-point link (so the two ends agree on scope), and the interface names, which depend on how many virtio adapters the template created. Match ens3 / ens4 to what the guest actually reports. 06 Static routing across three segments With three routers, static routes make the forwarding logic visible: each router only needs to know its directly connected subnets and a next hop for the rest. # r1: everything on the far side goes to r2 sudo ip route add 10.10.2.0/30 via 10.10.1.2 sudo ip route add 10.10.13.0/24 via 10.10.1.2 # r2: both LANs are behind neighbours sudo ip route add 10.10.11.0/24 via 10.10.1.1 sudo ip route add 10.10.13.0/24 via 10.10.2.2 # r3: mirror image of r1 sudo ip route add 10.10.1.0/30 via 10.10.2.1 sudo ip route add 10.10.11.0/24 via 10.10.2.1 # prove it, hop by hop ip route get 10.10.13.10 traceroute -n 10.10.13.10 ping -c2 10.10.13.10 A missing route shows up as "Destination Net Unreachable" or a silent timeout. Read ip route get on each hop before blaming GNS3: the emulator is almost never the problem when one subnet is unreachable. 07 Dynamic routing with FRR Once the static version works, replace the routes with a routing protocol and watch the tables build themselves. FRR installs from the distro and runs the same daemons as a real router. sudo apt install -y frr # enable the daemon before it will run sudo sed -i 's/^ospfd=no/ospfd=yes/' /etc/frr/daemons sudo systemctl restart frr sudo vtysh -c 'configure terminal' \ -c 'router ospf' \ -c 'network 10.10.0.0/16 area 0' \ -c 'exit' -c 'interface ens3' -c 'ip ospf area 0' \ -c 'exit' -c 'write memory' sudo vtysh -c 'show ip ospf neighbor' sudo vtysh -c 'show ip route ospf' Same area on every router for the first lab; multi-area is a second exercise. Announce only lab subnets. A stray default route can pull your management traffic into the emulator. Check adjacency before routes: no neighbour means no LSA exchange, and no routes to debug. If you only need to test reachability, static routes are more honest: you can see every decision. Use OSPF when convergence itself is the subject. 08 Testing routes the CCNA way The CCNA asks you to read a routing table and predict the path before you touch a cable. In the lab you can check that prediction in seconds — and explain why a /24 beat a /16 that was also in the table. # r2's whole world, on one screen ip route show # 10.10.1.0/30 dev ens3 proto kernel scope link src 10.10.1.2 # 10.10.11.0/24 via 10.10.1.1 dev ens3 # 10.10.13.0/24 via 10.10.2.2 dev ens4 # the decision for one destination, with the winning prefix ip route get 10.10.13.10 # 10.10.13.10 via 10.10.2.2 dev ens4 src 10.10.2.1 # the same question through FRR, with its own codes sudo vtysh -c 'show ip route 10.10.13.10' Candidate in r2's table Matches 10.10.13.10? Result 0.0.0.0/0 via 10.10.1.2 Yes, length 0 Loses to every more specific route 10.10.0.0/16 via 10.10.1.2 Yes, length 16 Loses to the /24 10.10.13.0/24 via 10.10.2.2 Yes, length 24 Wins: longest prefix match Longest match is decided by prefix length, not by the order routes were added and not by metric. Change the /24 to a /26 and watch a different rule take over. # two equal-cost paths, one prefix sudo ip route replace 10.10.13.0/24 \ nexthop via 10.10.2.2 dev ens4 nexthop via 10.10.1.2 dev ens3 ip route show 10.10.13.0/24 # both next hops are used; counters must move on both links # prove the loop, do not guess it ping -c1 -t 2 10.10.13.10 # From 10.10.2.1 icmp_seq=1 Time to live exceeded in transit traceroute -n -m 6 10.10.13.10 # drops and errors, per interface ip -s link show ens4 Test Command Pass Otherwise Reachability ping -c2 target Replies, 0% loss Route missing, ARP failing, or a firewall in the path Path traceroute -n target Hops in the planned order Asymmetric or looping path Decision ip route get target Expected next hop and source address Shadowed route or wrong prefix Longest match Add /16 and /24 for the same target /24 wins Table order or metric being blamed for prefix length ECMP Two next hops, then traffic Counters rise on both links One link dead, or hashing pinned to one path TTL ping -t 2 , increasing TTL exceeded names the loop's router Silent drop with no ICMP at all A ping proves the forward path, not the design Return traffic can take a different route and still succeed; the lab is only understood when both directions are captured. On FRR, compare show ip route (C/S/O codes and administrative distance: static 1, OSPF 110) with the kernel table ip route — they should agree, and when they do not, zebra is not installed the route you think it is. OSPF state Meaning in this lab Down No hello received; interface not in the area, or the link is down Init Hello seen, but this router is not in the neighbour's hello 2-Way Bidirectional on a broadcast segment; normal for non-DR/BDR ExStart / Exchange Leader election and database description exchange Loading LSAs requested; a stuck Loading is a database you need to read Full Databases synchronised — now routes can appear in show ip route ospf The prefix arithmetic and administrative-distance reasoning are worked through in the CCNA/CCNP manual ; the protocol-by-protocol background is in Networking . Run each test here until the answer is obvious before you read it. 09 Internet access without leaking A lab that needs package updates needs a path out, and a lab that needs to stay contained needs that path to be one-way and explicit. Put the NAT where you can see it — on the router that faces the host. # on the edge node, whose ens3 faces the GNS3 NAT/cloud node sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 sudo iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -o ens3 -j MASQUERADE sudo iptables -A FORWARD -i ens4 -o ens3 -s 10.10.11.0/24 -j ACCEPT sudo iptables -A FORWARD -i ens3 -o ens4 -d 10.10.11.0/24 \ -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT sudo iptables -P FORWARD DROP # verify from a LAN host ip route curl -sI https://deb.debian.org | head -1 Containment is part of the topology Forward policy DROP and a stateful allow rule are what keep the lab from becoming a router for your house. If the lab is for attack practice, isolate it completely and use a local package mirror — the defenders page explains why stray lab traffic is a detection story you do not want. 10 VLANs and switching A routed lab eventually needs a switch between routers, and a switched lab eventually needs VLANs. GNS3 ships an Ethernet switch node; verify its tagging options in your version, and use an Open vSwitch node when you need exact control. # inside an OVS node: two access ports and one trunk ovs-vsctl add-br br0 ovs-vsctl add-port br0 eth1 tag=10 ovs-vsctl add-port br0 eth2 tag=20 ovs-vsctl add-port br0 eth3 trunk=10,20 ovs-vsctl show Then address the VLANs on the router with sub-interfaces, and remember that the switch does not route: ip link add link ens4 name ens4.10 type vlan id 10 is what puts an address on a tag. 11 Capture and prove the path Right-click a link and start a capture: GNS3 shells out to dumpcap and shows the file in Wireshark. For anything scripted, take the pcap and read it yourself — the same discipline as the tcpdump manual. tshark -r link-r1-r2.pcapng -Y "icmp || ospf" -T fields \ -e ip.src -e ip.dst -e icmp.type -e ospf.msg | head -20 # the two counters that prove forwarding worked cat /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward nstat -az | grep -E "IpInReceives|IpOutRequests|IpInAddrErrors" Symptom on the wire What it means ICMP echo request arrives, no reply Return route missing on the far node OSPF hello one-way One interface not in the area, or MTU mismatch Repeated ARP for the gateway Wrong subnet mask, or gateway address typo Forty-byte window, no data MTU black hole; test with ping -M do -s 1400 Traffic only in one direction Only one link is captured — check the SPAN or the second cable For turning those captures into alerts, the Suricata build reads the same files offline; for the protocol background, the networking manual. 12 The paranoid checklist Check Pass condition KVM active /dev/kvm accessible; guest boot under ten seconds One subnet per link Addressing plan written; no overlap with the GNS3 management net Adapter count matches links No "interface not found" after adding a cable Forwarding on ip_forward=1 persisted in /etc/sysctl.d Routes readable ip route on each node shows only what you planned Return path tested traceroute works in both directions Forward policy explicit DROP default, stateful allow rules, no open MASQUERADE Capture kept Pcap plus the command that produced it, stored with the project Disk per node No two nodes share a writable qcow2 Project exported One archive you can rebuild from after a laptop dies 13 Common failures Symptom Cause Fix Node boots to a black console No getty on ttyS0 , or console type mismatch Add console=ttyS0 , enable the serial getty, reboot QEMU exits immediately Image path moved, or no KVM permission Check the template's disk path and ls -l /dev/kvm Only two NICs appear Template adapter count too low Edit the template, raise the count, restart the node Ping fails one way Missing return route or wrong netmask ip route get on both ends OSPF neighbour stuck in EXSTART MTU mismatch between neighbours Align MTU on both interfaces, or fix the virtual link MTU Everything is slow Software emulation, or too many vCPUs per node Enable KVM, reduce vCPU count, close the extra nodes LAN host has no internet NAT rule missing, forwarding off, or DNS absent Recheck MASQUERADE, ip_forward , and the resolver Lab traffic on the home network Cloud node bridged without a firewall Remove the bridge, use NAT with a DROP forward policy 14 Sources GNS3 — the official documentation, including QEMU templates and server setup. AV Dr. Alistair Vance & The Symbiotic Initiative Published October 2026 • Global Epistemology & Technology Review 00 Introduction: The Threshold of Co-Evolution Every major technological revolution in human history has forced a profound renegotiation of what it means to be human. The mastery of fire externalized survival; the printing press democratized cognition; the industrial engine augmented muscle. Today, artificial intelligence stands as the final frontier of tool-making: the externalization and scaling of cognition itself. Yet, public discourse remains gripped by a polarized paralysis—split violently between techno-utopians predicting an imminent paradise of automated leisure and catastrophists invoking deterministic dystopias of existential subjugation. Neither narrative captures reality. Artificial intelligence is neither a benevolent deity nor a rogue demonic entity; it is an algorithmic mirror forged from the cumulative history, data, biases, and brilliance of human civilization. It accelerates whatever dynamics we feed into it. Consequently, asking what AI will do to us is the wrong inquiry. The more urgent, uncomfortable question is: What must humanity fix within itself so that AI can elevate our species rather than automate our decay? 01 Part I: The Mirror of Intelligence When pruned of marketing hype, artificial intelligence offers unprecedented tools for civilizational uplift. By operating at combinatorial speeds impossible for biological neural networks, advanced models function across multiple transformative dimensions: 🧬 Cognitive & Scientific Synthesis Simulating complex biological pathways, protein folding, and material science discoveries in months instead of centuries, effectively compressing medical research timelines. ⚖️ Overcoming Psychological Biases Acting as an objective cognitive partner that challenges confirmation bias, analyzes systemic blind spots, and parses vast datasets free from emotional fatigue. 🕊️ Liberating Human Potential Automating bureaucratic drudgery and mechanical labor to redirect human bandwidth toward interpersonal empathy, philosophical inquiry, and creative expression. By absorbing the collective digital output of humanity, AI becomes an unsparing mirror. It reflects our cultural masterpieces alongside our historical prejudices, forcing us into a vital ontological awakening: to build a wise machine, we must confront the unresolved fractures in our own collective psyche. 02 Part II: The Reality Check Honesty demands that we confront the profound hazards and systemic frictions inherent in current AI trajectories. To romanticize artificial intelligence without acknowledging its structural pathologies is to invite catastrophe. Epistemic Drift and Hallucinations Unlike deterministic calculators, generative models synthesize probabilistic tokens based on patterns. When they invent false citations, logical fallacies, or authoritative falsehoods ("hallucinations"), they exploit human susceptibility to fluent authority—threatening to poison our epistemic commons with synthetic noise. Ecological and Energy Tolls Training and operating frontier foundation models requires staggering amounts of electrical power, specialized semiconductors, and fresh water for data center cooling. In an era of escalating climate crisis, unbridled compute scaling risks compounding ecological degradation unless decoupled from fossil fuels. The Concentration of Power and Moral Outsourcing AI development remains dangerously concentrated within a handful of monopolistic tech conglomerates backed by venture capital. Furthermore, humans increasingly suffer from moral outsourcing —delegating high-stakes judicial, medical, and ethical decisions to opaque algorithms to evade personal responsibility. The Danger of Opaque Agency "When we treat algorithms as infallible oracles rather than statistical instruments, we abdicate our moral duty and risk locking historical biases into immutable digital stone." 03 Part III: What Humans Must Improve to Elevate AI If artificial intelligence is to become a true catalyst for human flourishing rather than an amplifier of our worst impulses, humanity must undergo rigorous internal evolution. The engineering bottleneck is no longer solely in silicon; it is in human wisdom. 1. Epistemic Hygiene & Curation Shifting from gathering gargantuan unvetted datasets to curating high-integrity, ethically rigorous, and diverse knowledge corpora that prioritize truth over engagement metrics. 2. Rewriting Incentives Transitioning from attention-economy algorithms that monetize outrage and division toward alignment metrics that reward societal cohesion, scientific truth, and long-term sustainability. 3. Educational Reformation Upgrading global education away from rote memorization toward meta-cognition, rigorous skepticism, philosophical literacy, and emotional intelligence in an AI-saturated world. 4. Polycentric Governance Forging binding international treaties, transparent auditing frameworks, and inclusive global regulatory bodies that prevent unchecked corporate and nationalist arms races. Without cultivating deep emotional and philosophical maturity in our leaders, creators, and citizens, no amount of technical alignment mathematics will save us from our own short-sightedness. 04 Conclusion: The Mutual Ascent The symbiotic horizon is neither an inevitable utopia nor a guaranteed apocalypse; it is an ongoing, high-stakes negotiation between human consciousness and machine capability. As we refine our ethical frameworks, institutional resilience, and epistemic discipline, our tools will reflect that heightened wisdom back to us. The Reciprocal Evolution "We do not build AI to replace our humanity. We build AI to reveal what our humanity is truly capable of achieving when unburdened by unnecessary suffering and elevated by relentless truth." Conscious stewardship is our collective mandate. By stepping up to mend our own systemic flaws, we ensure that the dawn of artificial intelligence marks not the twilight of humanity, but the beginning of our greatest evolutionary leap.

A hands-on learning adventure · beginner to builder JavaScript From Zero to Hero A deep, friendly guide to thinking in code, making websites interactive, and understanding how JavaScript can also work outside the browser. No experience needed—just curiosity. 19 bite-sized lessons Examples from first steps to advanced No libraries needed Made for ages 12+ Your mission: Don’t memorize every word. Read a little, type the examples yourself, change them, break them, and fix them. That is how programmers learn. Ask a trusted adult before installing software or running code from strangers. 01 Think like a coder Programming is giving a computer clear instructions to solve a problem. A computer is very fast, but it does exactly what its instructions say—not what you meant. Coding is the art of turning a big idea into tiny, unambiguous steps. 🧩 1. Understand What should happen? What information do you have? What result do you want? 🪜 2. Break it down Split the job into smaller steps. A recipe is an algorithm: a list of steps in order. 🛠️ 3. Write and test Tell JavaScript the steps. Try normal, tiny, huge, and surprising inputs. 🔎 4. Improve Read what happened, fix one thing at a time, and make the code easier to understand. Algorithm before code: packing a school bag Look at tomorrow’s timetable. For each class, add its books and supplies. If it is sports day, add sports clothes. Check the list, then close the bag. Notice the words for each and if ? They become loops and decisions in code. Before typing, explain your solution in ordinary words or draw a flowchart. Vocabulary: An algorithm is a repeatable set of steps. A bug is a problem in a program. Debugging means finding and fixing that problem. Bugs are normal—even experts make them. 02 Your first JavaScript JavaScript (often shortened to JS) is a programming language that makes things happen. Try the browser console: in most desktop browsers, open Developer Tools and choose Console . Type a line and press Enter. On a phone or tablet, use an online coding environment with a trusted adult. The console is a scratchpad; it is not the same as a text message box. console.log("Hello, world!"); console.log(2 + 3); console.log() prints a value so you can inspect it. Text goes inside quotes; numbers do not. The semicolon marks the end of a statement. JavaScript often allows you to leave it out, but using it consistently can make code easier to scan. JavaScript is not Java Despite their similar names, Java and JavaScript are different languages, like a car and a carpet are different even though both start with “car”. This guide teaches JavaScript. Try it: Change the greeting to your name. Then print the answer to 12 * 4 . Predict the result before pressing Enter. 03 Values and variables Values are the information your program works with. Variables give useful names to information. Three useful ways to create a variable const learner = "Mina"; // This name should keep pointing to this value let score = 0; // This value can be updated score = score + 10; console.log(learner, score); Kind Use it when… Example const You won’t assign a different value to this variable. const homePlanet = "Earth"; let You need to assign a new value later. let lives = 3; lives = 2; var Mostly in older code; learn to recognize it, but usually prefer const or let . var oldStyle = true; A variable is like a labeled box, but const means the label cannot be pointed at a different value. If a const contains an object or array, the contents may still be changed; we will see why in Lesson 09. Common value types const username = "Kai"; // string: text const age = 12; // number: includes whole and decimal numbers const isReady = true; // boolean: true or false const score = null; // intentionally no value let nextMove; // undefined: no value assigned yet const huge = 12345678901234567890n; // bigint: very large whole number JavaScript also has symbol , used for special unique identifiers. You usually won’t need it at first. Check a value’s type with typeof —but be aware of one old JavaScript surprise: typeof null says "object" . console.log(typeof "hello"); // "string" console.log(typeof 42); // "number" console.log(typeof true); // "boolean" Text and templates const hero = "Nova"; const level = 4; const message = `${hero} reached level ${level}!`; console.log(message); Backticks create a template literal . The ${...} parts insert JavaScript values into the text. Changing values and naming let coins = 5; coins = coins + 2; // now 7 coins += 3; // now 10 coins++; // now 11 Use names that explain what a value means: minutesLeft is clearer than x . JavaScript names are case-sensitive: score and Score are different. 04 Math and comparisons Computers are great at arithmetic, counting, and checking rules. Operator Meaning Example result + Add, or join strings 7 + 2 → 9 - Subtract 7 - 2 → 5 * Multiply 7 * 2 → 14 / Divide 7 / 2 → 3.5 % Remainder after division 7 % 2 → 1 ** Power 3 ** 2 → 9 Order matters: multiplication and division happen before addition and subtraction. Use parentheses to make your meaning obvious: (2 + 3) * 4 . Equality and comparisons console.log(5 > 3); // true console.log(5 === 5); // true: same value and type console.log(5 === "5"); // false: number is not text console.log(5 !== 4); // true: not equal Prefer === and !== for equality. The older == can convert types in surprising ways, so beginners should avoid it until they understand coercion. Comparisons include < , > , <= , >= . Logic: combine yes/no answers const hasTicket = true; const isOldEnough = true; console.log(hasTicket && isOldEnough); // AND: both must be true console.log(hasTicket || isOldEnough); // OR: either can be true console.log(!hasTicket); // NOT: flips true/false Think of logic like rules for a game. && means “and”, || means “or”, and ! means “not”. JavaScript’s && and || can return one of their original values, not just true or false ; that shortcut is useful later. Averages and rounding const points = [8, 10, 6]; const total = points[0] + points[1] + points[2]; const average = total / points.length; console.log(Math.round(average)); // 8 Computers use floating-point numbers, so some decimal calculations are tiny bit inexact (for example, 0.1 + 0.2 ). For money, store cents as whole numbers where possible: 199 cents is $1.99. 05 Make decisions Programs choose different actions with conditions. const temperature = 18; if (temperature >= 25) { console.log("Warm day!"); } else if (temperature >= 15) { console.log("A light jacket might help."); } else { console.log("Bundle up!"); } JavaScript checks conditions from top to bottom and runs the first matching branch. Curly braces { } hold the instructions in a block. Indentation is not required by the computer, but it helps people see the structure. Switch for a list of exact choices const day = "Saturday"; switch (day) { case "Saturday": case "Sunday": console.log("Weekend!"); break; default: console.log("School day"); } break stops the switch from continuing into the next case. Values such as 0 , "" , null , undefined , and NaN act like false in a condition; most other values act like true. Count with a for loop for (let round = 1; round Read it as: start at 1; keep going while the condition is true; add 1 after each turn. The three parts are separated by semicolons. Watch the condition carefully: a mistake can cause an endless loop. Repeat while something is true let energy = 3; while (energy > 0) { console.log("Play!"); energy--; } A while loop checks before each turn. Make sure each turn can eventually make its condition false. Otherwise it may never stop. Loop through a collection const snacks = ["apple", "toast", "yogurt"]; for (const snack of snacks) { console.log(`Pack: ${snack}`); } for...of is a friendly way to visit each item in an array or other iterable. Use break to stop early or continue to skip to the next turn. Loop safety: If a page freezes, a loop might be running forever. Stop the page or close its tab. In your own code, double-check the starting value, stopping condition, and update. 07 Functions: reusable recipes A function groups instructions under a name. Give it inputs; it can return an output. function greet(name) { return `Hello, ${name}!`; } const greeting = greet("Sam"); console.log(greeting); name is a parameter —a named input. "Sam" is an argument —the actual value we pass in. return sends a result back. A function can also do a task without returning a useful value. Function expressions and arrow functions const double = function (number) { return number * 2; }; const triple = (number) => { return number * 3; }; const quadruple = number => number * 4; console.log(double(5), triple(5), quadruple(5)); Arrow functions are a shorter way to write many functions. If the arrow function has one expression, parentheses and braces can be shortened; that expression is returned automatically. Use braces plus return when the steps need more room. Default inputs and input checking function welcome(name = "friend") { return `Welcome, ${name}!`; } function add(a, b) { if (typeof a !== "number" || typeof b !== "number") { return "Please give me two numbers."; } return a + b; } console.log(welcome()); console.log(add(4, 6)); Keep each function focused: one clear job, a helpful name, and predictable inputs and outputs. This makes it easier to test and reuse. 08 Arrays: lists of things Use an array when you have an ordered list of values. const colors = ["teal", "gold", "violet"]; console.log(colors[0]); // "teal"; the first position is 0 console.log(colors.length); // 3 colors.push("coral"); // add to the end colors.pop(); // remove the last item Array positions are called indexes and start at zero. The last valid index is array.length - 1 . A const array can still have items added or removed: the variable still points at the same array. Useful array tools const numbers = [2, 4, 6, 8]; const doubled = numbers.map(number => number * 2); const bigOnes = numbers.filter(number => number >= 6); const found = numbers.find(number => number === 4); const total = numbers.reduce((sum, number) => sum + number, 0); console.log(doubled, bigOnes, found, total); Tool What it does Changes original? map Make a new array by changing each item No filter Make a new array with items that pass a test No find Get the first item that passes a test No reduce Combine items into one answer, such as a total No sort Reorder items (by default, as text) Yes For numbers, sort with a comparison rule: numbers.slice().sort((a, b) => a - b) . slice() makes a copy first, so the original list stays in its old order. Arrays of arrays const seats = [ ["A1", "A2"], ["B1", "B2"] ]; console.log(seats[1][0]); // "B1" 09 Objects: describe a thing An object groups named pieces of information, called properties. const pet = { name: "Pixel", kind: "cat", age: 3, isHungry: false }; console.log(pet.name); // dot notation console.log(pet["kind"]); // bracket notation pet.isHungry = true; Objects are useful when values belong together. A property’s name is its key . Use dot notation when you know the key; use brackets when you have the key in a variable or the name has special characters. Methods: functions that belong to objects const player = { name: "Rin", score: 0, earn(points) { this.score += points; return `${this.name} now has ${this.score} points.`; } }; console.log(player.earn(10)); In this method, this refers to the object that called it. this behaves differently in some kinds of functions; when that feels confusing, use a named parameter or read about arrow-function this rules later. Destructuring and spread const { name, score } = player; // take properties into variables const upgradedPlayer = { ...player, level: 2 }; // copy + add const newColors = [...["blue", "green"], "gold"]; // copy + add Objects are shared by reference: Assigning const otherPet = pet does not make a separate pet. Both names point to the same object. Spreading with { ...pet } makes a shallow copy: nested objects still need more care. JSON: a text format for data const saved = JSON.stringify(pet); // object → JSON text const restored = JSON.parse(saved); // JSON text → object JSON looks similar to JavaScript objects but is stricter: keys and text must use double quotes, and JSON cannot contain functions or undefined . Only parse JSON you trust or handle parse errors. 10 Scope, errors, and debugging Scope is where a name can be used. Debugging is careful detective work. const outside = "I can be used below"; function showMessage() { const inside = "I only exist in this function"; console.log(outside, inside); } showMessage(); // console.log(inside); // Error: inside is out of scope let and const are block-scoped: they live inside the nearest pair of braces where they were declared. Prefer small scopes and avoid reusing the same name for different ideas. Three kinds of problems Syntax error: the code is not written in a way JavaScript understands (perhaps a missing quote or bracket). Runtime error: the code starts, but something goes wrong while it runs. Logic bug: it runs, but gives the wrong answer. A calm debugging checklist Read the whole error message and note the line number. Check spelling, quote marks, brackets, and capitalization. Print intermediate values with console.log() . Test the smallest example that shows the problem. Change one thing, run again, and see whether it helped. Ask: what did I expect, what happened, and what is the first place they differ? function average(a, b) { const total = a + b; console.log("Checking total:", total); // temporary detective clue return total / 2; } console.log(average(8, 10)); Browser Developer Tools offer a debugger. Passive collection uses public records and third-party sources; active collection sends packets to the target and can be logged, rate-limited or reported. Do passive first, write down every source, and never let a scanner's timeout become a conclusion. 14 cards passive → active scope first Your recon is also evidence about you DNS queries, certificate-transparency lookups, user agents and scan sources are visible to the target and to third parties. Use infrastructure you are authorised to use, not a borrowed VPS, and never assume Tor makes an active scan anonymous — it usually makes it slower and more suspicious. nmap pkg: nmap What it does. The reference port scanner: host discovery, TCP/UDP port states, service and version detection, OS guesses and the NSE scripting engine. It is the tool you use to understand a host, not merely to find an open port. copy sudo nmap -sn 10.10.10.0/24 -oA evidence/scans/discovery sudo nmap -sS -p- --min-rate 1000 -oA evidence/scans/all-tcp 10.10.10.5 sudo nmap -sCV -p 22,80,443 --script safe -oA evidence/scans/services 10.10.10.5 Run it Broad discovery first, then all TCP ports, then a narrow service/script pass. Save with -oA ; a scan without output is a rumour. Use -Pn when ICMP is filtered, -T2 on fragile links, --reason to see why a port is marked open. Avoid -T5 on production or WAN links, --script vuln as a first move (noisy and occasionally disruptive), and UDP sweeps of entire ranges. Closed and filtered are different findings. Instead of masscan or rustscan for speed; nmap for truth. -sT works without raw sockets but is more connection-heavy; -sS is the usual choice when you have root. masscan pkg: masscan What it does. An asynchronous TCP port scanner with its own userland network stack. It trades accuracy and depth for raw speed across very large address ranges: no service detection, no scripts, no OS fingerprinting. copy sudo masscan -p1-65535 10.10.10.0/24 --rate=1000 \ --exclude 10.10.10.1 -oL evidence/scans/masscan.lst Run it Only on ranges you own or are authorised to test. Start at --rate 1000 , watch for packet loss, then verify every hit with nmap. Add --wait 3 so late replies are not lost. Avoid Internet-wide scans, rates that saturate a shared uplink, and treating a masscan miss as "closed". Its stack can be less reliable than the kernel's, especially behind NAT or stateful firewalls. Instead of Use it to find candidates across /16s and /8s; hand each live host to nmap. For a single host or a /24, rustscan is usually more convenient and nmap alone is already fast enough. rustscan pkg: rustscan What it does. Finds open TCP ports quickly, then automatically hands the open ports to nmap for service and script detection. Think of it as a fast front door with nmap waiting inside. copy rustscan -a 10.10.10.5 --ulimit 5000 -- -sV -sC -oA evidence/scans/rustscan Run it Everything after -- is passed to nmap. Raise --ulimit only on a machine you control. Use -b to tune batch size and --scan-order random to reduce obvious sequential patterns. Avoid Assuming its result is more accurate than nmap. It is a convenience wrapper; the nmap pass is what produces the evidence. Do not run high concurrency through a fragile VPN or IDS-heavy path. Instead of Use rustscan for a quick "which ports are open?" on one host; nmap directly when you need careful timing or complex NSE; masscan for enormous ranges. arp-scan pkg: arp-scan What it does. Discovers hosts on the local Layer-2 segment using ARP requests. Because ARP is not routed, it is authoritative only for the subnet you are plugged into — and it often finds devices that ignore ICMP. copy sudo arp-scan -I eth0 --localnet --retry 2 Run it Use --localnet or an explicit CIDR, and confirm the interface with ip -brief addr . Repeat once to catch sleeping devices. The vendor column comes from the MAC OUI and is a hint, not proof. Avoid Using it to infer hosts behind a router; ARP does not cross L3 boundaries. Do not confuse a silent host with an absent one — some stacks rate-limit ARP replies. Instead of nmap -sn is better for routed discovery; arp-scan is better for the local wire and for finding quiet appliances. Compare both before declaring a subnet empty. dnsrecon pkg: dnsrecon What it does. Enumerates DNS records and infrastructure: standard record types, zone-transfer attempts, SRV records, cache snooping and dictionary-based subdomain brute force. It is the quick, scriptable DNS check before a heavier mapping tool. copy dnsrecon -d example.com -t std --json evidence/recon/dnsrecon.json dnsrecon -d example.com -t brt \ -D /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-5000.txt Run it Start with -t std , then targeted -t axfr against each authoritative name server. Brute force only with permission and a sensible wordlist; use --threads conservatively so you do not poison your own resolver. Avoid Treating NXDOMAIN as proof a name does not exist (wildcards and split-horizon DNS exist), and brute-forcing a third-party domain you merely found in a certificate. Instead of dnsenum adds scraping and whois; fierce is lighter and focuses on non-contiguous IP space; amass is the deep mapping tool. dnsrecon is the fast first pass. dnsenum pkg: dnsenum What it does. A Perl-era DNS enumeration script: record lookups, zone-transfer attempts, subdomain brute force, reverse lookups and optional search-engine scraping. It remains useful because its output is compact and its zone-transfer routine is blunt. copy dnsenum --enum example.com \ -f /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-5000.txt -r Run it Use --enum as the shortcut and -r for recursive brute force. Save the terminal output; dnsenum's file output is less structured than dnsrecon's JSON. Avoid Relying on its Google scraping — search providers block or change formats constantly. Do not run recursion without a time limit; it can expand quickly. Instead of Prefer dnsrecon for clean JSON and current record types, or amass for a serious map. Keep dnsenum for a quick second opinion or an environment where it is already installed. fierce pkg: fierce What it does. A focused DNS reconnaissance tool for finding hosts in non-contiguous IP space: it resolves names, tests zone transfers, detects wildcards and brute-forces subdomains with a small, fast workflow. copy fierce --domain example.com \ --subdomains /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-5000.txt Run it Read the wildcard warning: if every random name resolves, brute-force results are meaningless until you filter the wildcard address. Keep the default timeouts for public DNS and raise them only in a lab. Avoid Using it as an attack tool — it is a resolver and a mapper. It will not find names that only exist in internal DNS, and it cannot see hosts that never appear in DNS. Instead of Faster to type than amass and cleaner than dnsenum for a single domain. Choose amass when you need certificates, ASNs, API sources and a graph; choose fierce for a five-minute answer. whois pkg: whois What it does. Queries the registration system for a domain, IP or ASN: registrar, creation and expiry dates, name servers, registrant organisation (when not redacted) and abuse contacts. RDAP is the modern JSON successor. copy whois example.com whois -h whois.iana.org example.com curl -s https://rdap.org/domain/example.com | jq '.events, .nameservers' Run it Query the authoritative registry for the TLD, then the registrar. Record the retrieval date; registration data goes stale. Use RDAP when you need machine-readable output. Avoid Trusting redacted fields or assuming the registrant is the operator. Privacy services, resellers and subsidiaries routinely hide the real owner. Do not use whois data for social engineering outside scope. Instead of DNS tells you what resolves now; whois tells you who registered it and when. They answer different questions and often disagree. theHarvester pkg: theharvester What it does. Collects public emails, hostnames, employee names and URLs from search engines, certificate transparency and other sources. It is contact-and-surface OSINT, not a port scanner. copy theHarvester -d example.com -b duckduckgo,bing,crtsh -l 300 \ -f evidence/recon/harvester Run it Use crtsh for certificate-history hostnames, and add API keys in /etc/theHarvester/api-keys.yaml for paid or rate-limited sources. Keep -l modest and save the HTML/JSON report. Avoid Assuming an email belongs to a current employee, or that a hostname still resolves. Verify before use. Respect provider terms and anti-spam law; harvested addresses are not a mailing list. Instead of amass maps infrastructure; theHarvester finds people and contact points; SpiderFoot automates both with correlation. Use the lightest one that answers the question. amass pkg: amass What it does. Maps an organisation's external attack surface: subdomains, IPs, ASNs, certificate names and relationships. Passive mode uses public sources; active mode adds DNS resolution, brute force and zone walking. copy amass enum -passive -d example.com -o evidence/recon/amass-passive.txt amass enum -active -d example.com -brute -w wordlist.txt \ -o evidence/recon/amass-active.txt Run it Passive first, always. Configure API keys in ~/.config/amass/config.yaml for better coverage, set -timeout , and keep the JSON output for the graph. Read the log: amass tells you which sources failed. Avoid Launching -active against a client's production DNS without warning — it is noisy. Do not assume the result is complete; private DNS, split horizon and CDNs hide whole estates. Instead of Use amass when scope is a whole organisation and you need relationships; dnsrecon/fierce for a quick domain check; theHarvester when the question is people, not infrastructure. recon-ng pkg: recon-ng What it does. LinuxIntroduction: Home Monkey Blog Introduction · one system, ten layers Linux, from the kernel out A Linux machine is not a desktop with hidden folders. It is a kernel, a tree of names, a table of processes and a set of permissions — and almost every mystery in /var/log is one of those four saying no. This page builds the model from the bottom: what a file really is, who a process is, how a service starts, and why chmod 777 never fixed anything. 1. A machine in layers Four layers matter, and each one has its own vocabulary. The kernel owns the hardware: it schedules the CPU, maps memory, talks to disks and exposes system calls. The C library and utilities turn those calls into programs. The init system (systemd on most distributions) starts and supervises everything else. The shell is just another program that reads text and calls fork and exec . Kernel Processes, memory, files, devices, network. It has no ls ; it has system calls such as openat , read , fork , execve and kill . Userland /bin , /usr/bin , libraries, the shell. Every command you type is a program that asks the kernel for something. Init PID 1. It starts services, evaluates targets, reaps orphans and is the parent of everything the boot produced. Distribution A packaging policy around the above: Debian's apt , Red Hat's dnf , Arch's pacman . Same kernel, different contracts. The practical consequence: when something “does not work”, decide which layer refused. A permission error is the kernel; a missing command is userland; a service that did not start is init; a package that cannot be installed is the distribution. 2. One tree: the file-system hierarchy Linux has a single namespace, rooted at / . Disks are not drives with letters; they are mounted onto empty directories. The Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS) explains why the same word, /etc , gives you the same kind of thing on every distribution. Where things live, and what breaks if you improvise Path Holds Rule / The root of everything; the first mount. Never fill it. Separate /var or /home when you can. /etc Host-specific configuration: fstab , ssh/sshd_config , systemd/ . Text, versioned in git, never binaries or state. /usr The distribution's userland: /usr/bin , /usr/lib , /usr/share . Package-owned. Do not drop files here by hand. /bin , /sbin Essential binaries; on modern systems symlinks into /usr . Must exist to boot and repair. /var Variable data: logs, caches, spools, databases, /var/lib . Grows without you. Watch it, do not delete blindly. /home , /root Users' files; root's own home is /root , not / . Backups belong here; secrets do not belong in world-readable homes. /tmp Temporary files, sticky bit, often cleared on boot. Never a permanent store; never a place for secrets. /opt , /srv Self-contained third-party software; data served by the host. Keep vendor trees out of /usr . /dev Device nodes and pseudo-devices: sda , null , tty , random . Managed by udev; do not create nodes by hand. /proc A live view of kernel and processes: /proc/1 , /proc/meminfo . Virtual: reads are questions, writes are commands. /sys Devices, buses and kernel objects as a tree of attributes. Virtual; used to read and tune hardware. /run Volatile runtime state: sockets, PID files, locks. tmpfs; empty after every boot. /mnt , /media Temporary mounts; removable media. Mount points, not storage. Two rules carry most of the weight. Configuration is separate from state ( /etc versus /var ), which is what makes a machine reproducible. And the package manager owns /usr : anything you compile yourself goes to /usr/local or /opt , or it will be overwritten or orphaned at the next upgrade. 3. Inodes, links and what a file is A directory is not a folder full of bytes; it is a table that maps names to inode numbers . The inode holds the metadata the kernel needs: type, mode, owner, group, size, timestamps, link count and the addresses of the data blocks. The name is not in the inode. That single sentence explains hard links, renames and why deleting a file can free nothing. $ ls -li notes.txt 131075 -rw-r--r-- 1 ana ana 2048 Oct 31 10:02 notes.txt $ stat notes.txt # inode, links, blocks, times $ find / -inum 131075 # every name pointing at that inode Hard links and symbolic links Hard link — a second name for the same inode, in the same filesystem. Both names are equal; the data disappears only when the link count reaches zero and no process holds it open. ln target newname . Symbolic link — a small file whose content is a path. It has its own inode, can cross filesystems, can dangle, and is resolved at access time. ln -s target newname . Consequences worth knowing before an incident: a hard link to a file with restrictive permissions gives you a second name but not new rights — permissions live in the inode, so they follow the link. A symlink in /tmp is an attack surface if a privileged program follows it blindly. And an open, deleted file still consumes disk: df shows the filesystem full while du cannot find the bytes, because the name is gone but the inode is alive. Find it with lsof +L1 and restart the holder. 4. Who may do what Every inode carries a mode: read (4), write (2), execute (1) for the user who owns it, the group it belongs to, and everyone else . For a directory the meaning shifts: read lists names, write creates and deletes entries, execute lets you traverse it. The mode in one line Octal Symbolic Meaning 644 -rw-r--r-- Owner writes, everyone reads. A normal document. 600 -rw------- Private: keys, tokens, personal data. 755 -rwxr-xr-x Executable programs and directories. 700 -rwx------ Private directory: nobody else may even list it. 640 -rw-r----- Owner writes, group reads; common for configs. 1777 drwxrwxrwt Shared directory with the sticky bit: delete only your own files ( /tmp ). 4755 -rwsr-xr-x setuid: the program runs with the file owner's effective UID ( passwd ). 2755 -rwxr-sr-x setgid: effective group of the file, or group inheritance in a directory. Umask, the permission you did not type New files start from a base (666 for files, 777 for directories) and the umask removes bits. A umask of 022 therefore yields 644 for files and 755 for directories; 077 yields 600 and 700. Change it per session with umask 077 and permanently in the login configuration, not by chmod-ing after the fact. When three classes are not enough, POSIX ACLs add per-user and per-group entries: setfacl -m u:bob:r-- report.txt , inspected with getfacl . When “root” is too much, capabilities split it: getcap and setcap cap_net_bind_service=+ep ./server lets one binary bind a privileged port without running as root. Both are still permissions, just finer-grained, and both are invisible to ls -l beyond a + or a capability set. 777 is not a fix. It is a decision to let any local account rewrite the file, and it usually hides a wrong owner, a wrong path, or a service running as the wrong user. Read the mode, the owner, the parent directory's execute bit and the ACL before changing anything. 5. Processes, PIDs and /proc A process is a running program with an address space, a set of open file descriptors and a kernel identity: the PID . PID 1 is the init system and cannot be killed like a normal process. Every other process has a parent ( PPID ); when the parent dies first, the child is re-parented to PID 1 or to the nearest subreaper, which is why “orphan” processes still show up. fork duplicates the current process, exec replaces its image with another program. A shell runs a command by forking and exec-ing; that is why a child's PID differs from the shell's, while the program's PID stays the same across exec . Threads share the address space and appear as tasks under /proc/PID/task . $ ps -eo pid,ppid,user,stat,cmd --sort=pid $ pstree -p 1 $ ls -l /proc/$$/fd # this shell's open descriptors $ cat /proc/1/cgroup # which cgroup the process is in $ lsof -p 4242 # files, sockets and pipes held open Zombie — the process has exited; its parent has not called wait . It holds a PID and a status, not memory. You cannot kill it; the parent must reap it (or be restarted). D state — uninterruptible sleep, usually waiting on I/O. Kill does nothing until the I/O returns. cgroups — how the kernel groups processes for CPU, memory and I/O limits; systemd uses them for every service. systemd-cgtop shows the tree. Namespaces — isolated views of PIDs, mounts, network and users; the foundation of containers. A container is a process with namespaces and cgroups, not a small virtual machine. /proc turns all of this into files: /proc/PID/cmdline , /proc/PID/environ , /proc/PID/fd , /proc/PID/status . Reading them is a legitimate, fast diagnosis; writing to some of them changes the running kernel. 6. Signals: how a process is asked to stop A signal is an asynchronous notification delivered by the kernel. Programs can catch, block or ignore most of them; two are reserved: SIGKILL and SIGSTOP cannot be caught, blocked or ignored, which is exactly why they are the last resort. The signals you will actually use Signal No. Meaning and habit SIGTERM 15 “Please shut down cleanly.” The default for kill and for systemd. Catchable, so the program can flush and close. SIGKILL 9 Immediate death, no cleanup, no handler. Leaves temp files, locks and half-written data. SIGINT 2 Ctrl-C in a normal terminal. Catchable; a TUI usually handles it as a key. SIGQUIT 3 Ctrl-\; often dumps core. SIGHUP 1 Terminal closed; conventionally “reload configuration”. Daemons reinterpret it. SIGSTOP / SIGCONT 19 / 18 Freeze and resume. STOP cannot be caught; a stopped process still holds memory and ports. SIGUSR1 / SIGUSR2 10 / 12 Application-defined: reopen logs, rotate, dump state. SIGCHLD 17 Child changed state; sent to the parent so it can reap. SIGWINCH 28 Terminal resized; TUIs redraw. Delivery is not a conversation: the sender gets success even if the receiver ignores the signal. A process that exits because of a signal reports status 128 + number — 137 for SIGKILL, 143 for SIGTERM. That is why a shell script's $? of 143 means “terminated”, not “failed with 143”. $ kill -TERM 4242 # ask $ kill -KILL 4242 # insist, after giving it a moment $ pkill -TERM -u www-data nginx $ kill -l # the whole list 7. Services, targets and systemd Older systems used SysV runlevels 0–6. systemd replaced them with targets : named groups of units that pull in other units. The old numbers survive as compatibility aliases ( runlevel3.target ), but the model is a dependency graph, not a numbered ladder. Targets you will meet Target Old runlevel What it means poweroff.target 0 Shut down. rescue.target 1 Single user, root shell, minimal services. multi-user.target 3 Networking and services, no graphical session. The normal server default. graphical.target 5 Multi-user plus a display manager. reboot.target 6 Reboot. systemctl get-default prints the target the machine boots into; systemctl isolate rescue.target switches at runtime; systemctl set-default multi-user.target makes it permanent. A unit is a contract, not a script [Unit] Description=Backup worker After=network-online.target [Service] Type=simple User=backup ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/backup --once Restart=on-failure RestartSec=5 NoNewPrivileges=yes [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target Unit types cover more than daemons: .service (a process), .socket (activation on connection), .timer (a schedule, replacing cron), .mount and .automount , .target (a group), .slice (a cgroup subtree), .path (watch a path). systemctl start x runs it now; enable only wires it into a target for the next boot; enable --now does both; mask makes it impossible to start. After editing a unit: systemctl daemon-reload , then restart . Without the reload systemd runs the old definition and the file looks correct while behaviour is stale. systemctl status x gives state, PID, cgroup and the last log lines; journalctl -u x -b gives the history of this boot. systemctl cat x shows the unit plus drop-ins; systemctl edit x creates an override in /etc/systemd/system/x.service.d/ instead of editing the package's file. Units live in /usr/lib/systemd/system (packages) and /etc/systemd/system (the administrator). The latter wins. On stop, systemd sends SIGTERM , waits (default 90 s, TimeoutStopSec ), then SIGKILL . A service that “takes ten seconds to die” usually ignores SIGTERM; fix the handler rather than lowering the timeout. 8. Devices, hardware and modules Hardware is not addressed by name. The kernel exposes devices as files in /dev with a major number (which driver) and a minor number (which instance). ls -l /dev/sda shows 8, 0 ; udev creates the names and the symlinks ( /dev/disk/by-uuid/… ) when the device appears. Discs and partitions lsblk -f , blkid , findmnt . Mounts are declared in /etc/fstab and activated with mount -a or a systemd .mount unit. Buses lspci -k , lsusb , lscpu . The -k flag names the kernel driver in use. Kernel messages dmesg -T (timestamps) shows detection, firmware and driver errors. It is the first place to look when a device is missing. Modules lsmod , modinfo , modprobe . Persistent module options go in /etc/modprobe.d/ , not in a shell script. /sys is the same hardware as a tree of attributes: read /sys/class/net/eth0/mtu , write to it to change it (or use ip , which does both sides properly). /proc answers kernel questions ( meminfo , loadavg , interrupts ), /sys answers device questions, /dev is the device itself. The distinction that saves time in an incident: hardware is what the kernel detected, software is what the distribution installed, and configuration is what you changed. A missing interface can be any of the three — check dmesg , lspci -k and ip link before reinstalling anything. 9. Software and packages On Debian and Ubuntu, dpkg owns the installed database and apt resolves dependencies and fetches from repositories. On Red Hat and Fedora, rpm and dnf play the same roles. A repository entry is a promise about signatures and versions; a .deb downloaded from a blog is not. # Debian / Ubuntu apt update && apt upgrade apt install nginx dpkg -S /usr/sbin/nginx # which package owns this file apt-file search nginx.conf # which package would provide it # Red Hat / Fedora dnf install nginx rpm -qf /usr/sbin/nginx What lives where, once installed Place Content Who owns it /usr/bin , /usr/lib Distribution binaries and libraries. The package manager. /usr/local Locally compiled software, by convention prefix --prefix=/usr/local . You. Never overwritten by packages. /opt Vendor trees that bring their own layout (browsers, agents). The vendor's installer. /etc Configuration files, often marked .dpkg-dist during upgrades. The package initially, you afterwards. /var/lib State: databases, package lists, service data. The service; back it up deliberately. /var/log Text logs and archives; journald's binary store is /var/log/journal . Log rotation, not you. Upgrades are not the only lifecycle: pin a version when a service depends on it, read the changelog before a major jump, and keep configuration in version control so the question “what changed?” has an answer other than memory. 10. Logs, boot, and a checklist The journal is the default log sink: structured, indexed and queried with journalctl . Text files under /var/log still exist and still matter (nginx, application logs, auth.log on Debian). $ journalctl -b -p err # this boot, errors and worse $ journalctl -u nginx --since "1 hour ago" $ journalctl -k # kernel messages only $ journalctl --disk-usage A normal boot is a chain: firmware → bootloader → kernel and initramfs → PID 1 → target → units. systemd-analyze , systemd-analyze blame and systemctl list-units --failed locate the slow or broken link. If the graphical target never arrives, ask which unit failed, not which pixel is missing. The ten-minute checklist Which layer? Kernel ( dmesg ), userland ( command -v ), init ( systemctl status ), package ( dpkg -S ). Is the file there, with which mode and owner? ls -l , stat , getfacl . Can the service's user reach it? Check every directory on the path, not just the file. Is the process running, and as whom? ps -o user,pid,ppid,stat,cmd -p PID , /proc/PID/status . Did it die from a signal? Exit status 137/143, journalctl -u . Is it enabled for the next boot? systemctl is-enabled , is-active . Is the disk full? df -h , df -i (inodes), lsof +L1 (deleted open files). Is the device seen? lsblk , lspci -k , dmesg -T . What changed? Package history, configuration diff, unit drop-ins. Write it down. The next person will be you, six months later. None of this requires memorising flags. It requires keeping four models straight: the tree, the inode, the process and the unit. Once those are clear, most “Linux problems” become a sentence you can finish: the service cannot read its key because it runs as www-data , the file is 600 root:root , and the directory above it is 700 . MathQuest: MathQuest Home Start Maths, from the very beginning We begin with stones and sheep. No symbols yet, no test, no hurry. Press Next and take the first small step. If a word is new, it will be explained before you use it. Counting One stone, one sheep A shepherd put one stone in a bag for every sheep leaving in the morning. At night, one stone came out for every sheep coming home. If a stone was left, a sheep was missing. That is counting: one thing for one thing. Names Numbers are names for groups We give the groups names in a fixed order: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten. Say them out loud now. The last name you say is how many there are. Zero Zero is a number too An empty basket has 0 apples. Zero is not a mistake and not “nothing at all”: it is the number that says the basket is empty. It will behave very well when we start adding and multiplying. Your turn Count these dots ● ● ● ● ● How many dots are there? Comparing More, fewer, the same Put one dot on each apple. If dots are left over, there are more dots than apples. If apples are left over, there are more apples. If nothing is left on either side, they are equal. No numbers needed — just matching. Adding What does “to add” mean? To add means to put groups together and count the whole pile. The sign is + , and the answer is called the sum . “To sum” means “to add up”. ● ● ● + ● ● = ● ● ● ● ● Three apples and two apples make five apples: 3 + 2 = 5 . Your turn Add four and three Start at 4 and count three more: five, six, seven. 4 + 3 = ? Subtracting What does “to subtract” mean? To subtract means to take some away and count what is left. The sign is − , and the answer is called the difference . You have 5 sweets and eat 2: 5 − 2 = 3 . The difference is 3 sweets. Subtracting is the undo of adding. 9 − 4 = ? Multiplying What does “to multiply” mean? To multiply means to add the same amount again and again. Instead of 4 + 4 + 4 , we write 3 × 4 : three groups of four. The answer is called the product . ● ● ● ● ● ● ● ● ● ● ● ● 2 × 5 = ? Dividing What does “to divide” mean? To divide means to share into equal groups. The sign is ÷ , and the answer is called the quotient . Twelve sweets among three friends: 12 ÷ 3 = 4 . Sometimes one is left over: 7 ÷ 2 = 3 remainder 1 . The leftover is called the remainder . 10 ÷ 2 = ? Well done You have used all four Plus, minus, times, divide. Nobody is born knowing them, and nobody learns them by reading once. Everybody learns them by doing one more. Wrong answers are free here. They are how the next step becomes easy. Place value Why ten is special Ten ones bundle into one ten. So 23 means two tens and three ones, and 45 means four tens and five ones. Four tens and five ones make which number? Fractions Parts of one thing Cut a pizza into 4 equal slices. One slice is 1/4 . The bottom number says how many parts, the top says how many you take. Two slices are 2/4 , which is the same as one half. Your turn Half a pizza How many quarters make a half? Percent Parts of a hundred 50% is half, 25% is a quarter, 100% is all of it. The sign % simply means “out of a hundred”. 50% of 10 = ? Algebra A box with a secret Three plus a hidden number equals seven. What is in the box? Four. We write the box as x : 3 + x = 7 . That sentence is called an equation , and finding the box is called solving it. x + 2 = 6. What is x? Geometry Fence and floor Perimeter is the fence around a shape. Area is the floor inside it. A square 3 metres by 3 metres has area 9 square metres. A rectangle is 2 by 5. Its area? Chance How likely is it? A die has six faces, and three of them are even. So an even number comes up 3 out of 6 times, which is one half. That is probability : the good outcomes divided by all the outcomes. Change Speed and change A car covers 100 km in 2 hours, so it averages 50 km per hour . That is division doing real work. Calculus asks a sharper question: how fast was it going at one exact instant? It answers by making the time smaller and smaller. Functions A function is a machine Put a number in, get one number out, always by the same rule. y = 2x + 1 says: double it, then add one. Put in 3, out comes 7. y = 2x. If x = 4, what is y? Graphs A rule drawn as a picture Draw every input on the flat line and its output going up. The points of y = 2x + 1 form a straight line. How steep the line is, is called the slope . A flat line means nothing changes; a steep line means it changes fast. Powers and roots Multiplying a number by itself 2 × 2 × 2 is written 2³ and equals 8. The small 3 is the exponent . A root goes back: √9 = 3 , because 3 × 3 = 9. 3² = ? Quadratics The curve of a thrown ball When the rule has an x² in it, the picture becomes a U-shaped curve called a parabola . A ball thrown into the air follows one: up, then down. Where the curve crosses the ground — where the output is zero — is what solving a quadratic means. Trigonometry Measuring what you cannot reach In a right triangle the ratios between the sides depend only on the angle. Sine is the side opposite the angle divided by the longest side. With that ratio and one measured angle you can find the height of a tree, a tower, or a mountain, without climbing it. A right triangle has opposite 3 and longest side 5. What is the sine? Sequences and limits Patterns that keep going 2, 4, 6, 8… adds two each time. 1, 2, 4, 8… doubles. A sequence is a list with a rule. A limit asks where the list is heading, even if it never quite arrives. It is how mathematics talks about “getting closer and closer”. What comes next: 3, 6, 9, 12, ? Calculus Change at an instant, and area under a curve A derivative is the speed of change at one exact moment. An integral adds up thin slices to measure an area. They undo each other, and between them they describe falling bodies, cooling coffee, growing populations and the shape of a curve. Vectors and matrices Arrows and grids of numbers A vector is an arrow: it has a length and a direction. Wind, force and speed are vectors. A matrix is a grid of numbers that moves every point of a picture at once — the maths behind turning a 3D model on a screen. Statistics What a crowd of numbers says The mean adds everything and divides by how many there are. For 2, 4 and 6 the mean is 4. What is the mean of 2, 4 and 6? Physics Where the rules meet the world Force is mass times acceleration: F = m × a . Voltage is current times resistance: V = I × R . Energy is power times time. Every one of them is multiplication and division wearing a lab coat. Mass 2, acceleration 3. What is the force? Proof Why something is true A proof is an argument with no gaps: it starts from what is already known and ends at the claim. One counterexample is enough to prove a sentence false. “Every odd number is prime” sounds fine until 9: odd, and 3 × 3. One example, and the sentence falls. The road ahead What comes next, in one line each Fractions, decimals, percent — the same part written three ways. Powers and roots — multiplying a number by itself. Algebra — letters as boxes, solved by keeping both sides equal. Functions and graphs — a rule drawn as a picture. Geometry — angles, area, volume, Pythagoras. Trigonometry — the ratios inside right triangles. Probability and statistics — chance and what a crowd of numbers says. Sequences and limits — patterns that go on forever, approached. Derivatives and integrals — change at an instant, and area under a curve. Vectors, matrices, proof — shape in numbers, and why something is true.
